name: Secret
epitaph: It couldn't keep a secret. Or its users.
oneLiner: An app where you posted anything anonymously and it was shown to your friends and their friends, without your name.
causeOfDeath: Anonymity attracted gossip and bullying, growth stalled, a Yik Yak copy redesign failed, and the founder chose to close and return the cash.
moneyNote: $35M raised (TechCrunch). Valuation after the July 2014 round reported as 'more than $100M' (TechCrunch later said $120M). Closed; leftover cash returned to investors.
inOneMinute: Secret let you post **anonymously to your friends**. Silicon Valley loved it in 2014, and it raised $35 million within about a year.
In the same round, **each co-founder sold $3 million of their own shares**, while the app earned no revenue. Staff found out later.
Posts turned mean, growth stalled and a redesign copying Yik Yak failed. In April 2015 the founder **shut it and gave investors their money back**.
killerLine: When your product's best feature is also its biggest danger, **you must design the safety in before you scale**.

numbers.label: taken off the table by the two founders
Snapchat's offer that Secret's side turned down

chapters.title: The idea: honest words, no names
chapters.body: David Byttow had spent five years at Google and almost a year at Square. Chrys Bader-Wechseler was a former Google product manager. In late 2013 they built Secret. You wrote a short post, put a pretty background behind it, and it went to your phone contacts and their friends. **Your name was never shown.** Byttow believed people would be more honest and creative if they didn't have to fear judgement. In early 2014, Secret spread like wildfire inside Silicon Valley. Tech workers used it to share office gossip, rumours about startups and personal confessions. Big investors such as Kleiner Perkins and Google Ventures backed it early.

chapters.title: The rise: hot money, fast
chapters.body: Secret raised $8.6 million in March 2014, when it had only three employees. In July 2014 it raised **$25 million more**, led by Index Ventures, valuing the company at more than $100 million. During that round, **Byttow and Bader-Wechseler each sold $3 million of their own shares** for cash. This is called a secondary sale (selling existing shares instead of the company issuing new ones). The app still earned no revenue. According to reports, the founders hadn't told employees, and some found out through posts on Secret itself. Around the same time, Snapchat's Evan Spiegel offered **$50 to $60 million** to hire the team. Secret's investors wanted more, and the talks died.

chapters.title: The cracks: anonymity turns ugly
chapters.body: Anonymity cut both ways. Many posts were, in Secret's own words, "defamatory, offensive, or mean-spirited". A false rumour that Evernote was being sold spread through the app. In August 2014, **a court in Brazil ordered Apple and Google to remove Secret** from their app stores there, over fears that it encouraged cyberbullying. Meanwhile growth slowed. In December 2014 the team relaunched Secret with a plain, text-only design that critics called **a copy of Yik Yak**, a rival anonymous app. It didn't work. Usage kept falling. In January 2015, Bader-Wechseler stepped down after disagreements about the direction. In the following months, nearly all of Secret's top engineers left.

chapters.title: The fall: an honest goodbye
chapters.body: By April 2015, a company that had over 20 staff a few months earlier had fewer than 10, and the app had dropped out of the top 1,000 US apps. On 29 April 2015, Byttow announced he was shutting Secret down. He wrote that it **"does not represent the vision I had when starting the company"**. Instead of spending the rest of the money on another pivot (a big change of direction), he chose to **return the remaining cash to investors**, which is rare in startups. He called it the hardest decision of his life. Reports later said his red Ferrari, bought after the share sale, had been sold too.

timeline.event: Secret, still in stealth, raises its first seed money

mistakes.title: Scaled anonymity without strong safety
mistakes.explain: Secret's core feature, no names, also invited rumours and bullying. The company itself admitted many posts were mean or defamatory. **A court in Brazil ordered the app removed.** Safety tools came after the damage, not before. When the people who use your app feel unsafe or disgusted, they quietly stop opening it.

mistakes.title: Founders cashed out before the company worked
mistakes.explain: Each co-founder sold $3 million of shares in mid-2014, while Secret had **no revenue and an unproven future**. Some staff learned of it only later and felt the founders were protecting themselves against failure. Whatever the intent, it damaged trust inside the team just as the hard part began.

mistakes.title: Copied a rival instead of fixing the core
mistakes.explain: When growth slowed, Secret relaunched with a minimal, text-only design that critics called **a clone of Yik Yak**. It didn't bring users back. Copying a competitor's look rarely fixes a deeper problem, which here was that people no longer enjoyed what they found in their feed.

mistakes.title: Turned down a soft landing
mistakes.explain: Snapchat offered $50 to $60 million to hire the team. Investors wanted closer to the $120 million valuation, and the talks ended. One source later called it **"the beginning of the end of Secret."** A high valuation can make a sensible exit look like a loss, until the company is worth nothing.

warningSigns: Is a growing share of your content mean, false or unsafe while you keep pushing for growth?
Did your usage spike for a month after launch and then quietly start falling?
Would your team be upset if they learned what the founders are doing with their own shares?
Are you redesigning to look like a competitor rather than fixing why users leave?
Are your best engineers leaving one by one?

lessons.title: Build safety before you build reach
lessons.detail: If your app has anonymous posts, comments or DMs, add reporting, blocking and moderation on day one. Write rules about bullying before your first 1,000 users, not after a court case.

lessons.title: Hype in your city is not a market
lessons.detail: Secret exploded inside Silicon Valley because tech people loved gossiping about tech. Before raising big money, check that people outside your bubble use it every week.

lessons.title: Be open with your team about money
lessons.detail: If founders ever sell some shares, tell the team yourself, early, and explain why. People forgive a lot, but not finding out from a rumour.

lessons.title: Don't let a valuation block a good exit
lessons.detail: A $120M valuation is just a price on paper. If a real offer can protect your team and investors, weigh it against the honest chance your company survives alone.

lessons.title: Closing well is a skill
lessons.detail: Byttow closed early and returned leftover money, which kept his reputation alive: his next startup was later acqui-hired by Postmates. If it's over, end it cleanly and honestly.

quote.text: I believe in failing fast in order to go on and make only new and different mistakes.
quote.who: David Byttow, Secret co-founder and CEO
quote.context: In his post announcing Secret's shutdown, April 2015

afterlife.text: Secret wound down over about two weeks in May 2015 and returned its leftover money to investors. Byttow started a new project called Bold, which Postmates acqui-hired in June 2017; he later joined Snap as director of engineering in 2018. In 2018, TechCrunch revealed how close Snapchat came to buying the Secret team in 2014.
